segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Come, I will show you the judgment on the great prostitute who sits on many waters,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: with whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality, and those who live on the earth became drunk on the wine of her sexual immorality.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness. And I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman was clothed in purple and scarlet and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, and she held in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: “Babylon the Great, the mother of prostitutes and of the abominations of the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw the woman drunk on the blood of the holy ones and on the blood of the witnesses of Jesus. And when I saw her, I was greatly amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the angel said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Why are you amazed? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, the one that has the seven heads and the ten horns.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss, and it goes to destruction. And those who live on the earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will be amazed when they see the beast, because it was, and is not, and will come.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: This calls for a mind that has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. They are also seven kings:

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he comes he must remain only a little while.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And the beast that was and is not is itself an eighth, and it is one of the seven, and it goes to destruction.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: These have one purpose, and they give their power and authority to the beast.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: These will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to me,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And the ten horns that you saw, and the beast—these will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and they will eat her flesh and burn her up with fire,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose, and to act with one purpose and give their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: And the woman that you saw is the great city that has royal power over the kings of the earth.”

notes.note: The phrase echoes Jeremiah 51:13, where historical Babylon, built on the Euphrates and its canals, is addressed as the one who lives “by many waters.” The angel gives the waters a symbolic meaning in verse 15.

The Greek noun and its verb are cognate with the word for “prostitute” in verse 1 and cover prostitution and illicit sex generally; older versions have “whore” or “harlot” and “fornication.” In the Hebrew prophets the image is used of cities and peoples for idolatry and for corrupting political and commercial entanglements, and most interpreters take it in that figurative sense here.

The Greek has no article and could also be read “in spirit,” meaning in a visionary state as opposed to bodily travel. The same phrase marks the main visions of the book (1:10; 4:2; 21:10), and most translations take it as a reference to God’s Spirit.

The word may be part of the inscription itself (“Mystery, Babylon the Great,” as in the King James Version) or a comment that the name has a hidden, symbolic meaning. The second reading is followed here, as in most recent translations: the name is not literal Babylon, and the angel goes on to explain it in verses 7–18.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

The Greek word means “witness,” one who testifies. Because these witnesses have been killed, many versions use “martyrs,” the English word that descends from it, but the narrowing of the term to “one who dies for the faith” is generally thought to be later than Revelation, or only just beginning in it. The genitive can mean witnesses belonging to Jesus or witnesses who testify to him.

notes.phrase: was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss
notes.note: The threefold description deliberately mimics the title of God in this book, “the one who is and who was and who is coming” (1:4, 8; 4:8). The beast is presented as a counterfeit of God, but its formula has “is not” in the middle and ends in destruction.

The Greek word covers both mountains and hills, and some translations have “seven hills.” Rome was proverbially the city on seven hills, and most scholars think first-century readers would have recognized the allusion at once. A minority take the mountains purely as symbols of kingdoms or powers.

The identity of the seven kings is disputed. Many scholars see a sequence of Roman emperors, though they differ on where to begin counting and whom to include, and many connect the beast that “is one of the seven” in verse 11 with the contemporary rumor that Nero would return. Others take seven as a symbolic number for the complete span of oppressive rule rather than a list to be decoded.

The Greek word can mean a realm or the rule and status of a king. Here and in verses 17 and 18 it is something received, handed over, and held over other kings, so the sense is kingship rather than territory. Older versions have “kingdom” in verses 12 and 17 and “reigns” in verse 18; several modern versions use “royal power” or “dominion.”

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a battle or contest. “Overcome,” used by the King James Version and several modern versions, now tends to suggest merely getting past a difficulty; “conquer” keeps the note of victory and the link with the promises to “the one who conquers” in chapters 2–3. The meaning is not in dispute.

notes.phrase: those with him are called and chosen and faithful
notes.note: The Greek has no verb in this clause. It can be read as a description of the Lamb’s companions, as here, or as saying that they share in the victory: “and those with him, the called and chosen and faithful, will conquer too.” Translations are divided.

The same Greek word is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in the New Testament where it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation’s recurring lists of peoples, nations, and languages, the scope is the whole world.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Acts, Paul, and Revelation in literal and figurative senses, and translators vary between fornication, sexual immorality, prostitution, and unchastity; the verb πορνεύω should be fixed with it.
Versions split between whore, harlot, and prostitute across the Gospels, 1 Corinthians, Hebrews, James, and Revelation, and the choice sets the tone of Revelation 17–19.
The word shifts between realm, reign, and kingship throughout the New Testament, and the line between “kingdom” and “royal power” or “reign” needs one rule.
Translators vary between witness and martyr where the witness has been killed (Acts 22:20; Revelation 2:13; 17:6), and readers should see one policy.
Occurs in the Gospels (“abomination of desolation”), Luke 16:15, and Revelation, and versions vary between abomination, detestable thing, and obscenity.
